newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cautiously optimistic on India-Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cautiously optimistic on India-Pakistan.

text.p: U.S. officials and private analysts are voicing cautious optimism about a possible thaw in relations between historic rivals Pakistan and India.
But Washington has played down hopes for any breakthrough at a senior-level dialogue due to resume on March 28 in New Delhi after a three-year suspension.

"We and many other well-wishers hope both countries will take full advantage of this opportunity to resume a serious high-level dialogue," the State Department's top policymaker for the region, Robin Raphel, said.

"Without regular communication, there can be no enduring trust. The agenda for potentially productive negotiations is immense," Raphel, assistant secretary of state for South Asian Affairs, told the House of Representatives subcommittee on Asia and the Pacific on March 12.

Another State Department official described the talks, at the foreign secretary level, as a "new window of opportunity" opened by Pakistan Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, who took office in February, and his Indian counterpart H.D. Deve Gowda, who took office last June.
"The level of invective has been lowered," said the official. "That's a positive development."

In a downbeat assessment shortly before Sharif was sworn in as prime minister, the acting director of central intelligence, George Tenet, discounted prospects for reduced tension between India and Pakistan, which have fought three wars since independence from Britain and partition 50 years ago.

"Relations between India and Pakistan remain poor, and we see few signs that point toward a serious thaw," Tenet, now President Bill Clinton's nominee to be the next CIA director, told the Senate Armed Services Committee.
"Although neither side wants war, the two rivals could stumble into it, most likely as a result of misperceptions of each others' intentions or military posture," he said.
Tom Crispell, a CIA spokesman, declined to add or subtract from Tenet's testimony based on late developments this week.

The top U.S. concern in South Asia is the prevention of nuclear and ballistic missile proliferation and the reduction of tension between India and Pakistan, which centre on their competing claims to Kashmir.
Kashmir has been divided by a military line of control since 1948 into the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir and Pakistan-controlled Azad (Free) Kashmir.

India blames Pakistan for supporting a separatist movement active in the Moslem-dominated Kashmir Valley since 1990. Pakistan claims to lend only moral and political support to the rebellion while accusing India of creating dissension in Pakistan's southern Sindh province, which borders India.

In its talks with India and Pakistan, the United States has urged the opening of a dialogue on Kashmir initially leading to the demilitarization of the Siachen Glacier area; a mutual reduction of conventional arms and defence expenditures; and an agreement by both countries to stop involving themselves in each other's regional unrest.

Selig Harrison, a guest scholar on the region at the Woodrow Wilson International Centre for Scholars, said one promising factor was that influential elements in Pakistan, including industrial leaders, had begun mulling opening trade with India.
"Until now, Pakistan has almost unanimously believed that opening up trade would lead to being swamped by India economically," he said in an interview.

"What we have to watch for in these negotiations between the two foreign secretaries is whether they talk about trade at all and whether they discuss compromises on both sides that would make possible greater trade," he said. "There's almost none now."
